rules.source: Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (assented August 11 2023); DPDP Rules, 2025 notified November 14 2025, fully operationalizing the Act. Official: Ministry of Electronics and IT (MeitY), https://www.meity.gov.in/
rules.retrieved_snippet: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (DPDP Act) received the assent of the President on 11th August 2023... The Government of India notified the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Rules, 2025 on 14 November 2025, marking the full operationalisation of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023.

rules.source: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012 (as amended 2019) — Section 12 covers online sexual harassment of a child, Section 13 covers use of a child in media for sexual gratification; the DPDP Act, 2023 separately requires verifiable parental consent for processing a child's personal data. Official press release (PIB, Ministry of Law and Justice): https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2245026&reg=3&lang=1
rules.retrieved_snippet: Section 12 punishes sexual harassment of a child, including through electronic or online means, such as making sexually coloured remarks, showing pornographic material, or repeatedly contacting a child with sexual intent. Section 13 criminalises the use of a child in any form of media for the purpose of sexual gratification. The 2019 Amendment introduced stricter punishments.

rules.source: Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (Act No. 35 of 2019), assented August 9 2019, in force since July 2020, replacing the Consumer Protection Act 1986. No single official full-text government URL was retrieved in this search pass — verify against India Code (indiacode.nic.in) before relying on this.
rules.retrieved_snippet: The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (Act No. 35 of 2019) was passed by Lok Sabha on 30 July 2019, by Rajya Sabha on 6 August 2019, and assented to by President Ram Nath Kovind on 9 August 2019, commencing on 20 July 2020 and 24 July 2020. It repeals and replaces the Consumer Protection Act, 1986.

rules.source: India has no standalone AI-specific statute as of 2026; the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 is the primary law shaping AI regulation (AI systems processing personal data fall under its obligations/restrictions), alongside existing IT Act 2000 and copyright law. Secondary summary: https://www.ibanet.org/Building-AI-strategies-according-to-new-data-framework-india — honest gap, not filled with an invented AI-specific law.
rules.retrieved_snippet: Regarding AI regulation, the DPDP Act is set to help shape India's artificial intelligence landscape, in addition to India's existing copyright and information technology laws, with the Indian government not foreseeing the creation of a standalone AI law. AI systems process large volumes of personal data, and as a result, the providers of AI systems will inevitably be subject to the obligations and restrictions outlined in the DPDP Act.

rules.source: Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 (RPWD Act), in effect since 19 April 2017 — Section 42 mandates equal ICT access (websites, digital content, electronic media); Section 46 requires accessible government digital services. Guidelines for Indian Government Websites (GIGW) enforce WCAG 2.1 Level AA for public-sector platforms; Bureau of Indian Standards IS 17802 (24 Dec 2021) aligns national ICT accessibility standards with WCAG. Non-compliance penalties INR 10,000-500,000. Secondary summary: https://www.deque.com/blog/how-the-rights-of-persons-with-disabilities-act-rpwd-impacts-digital-accessibility-in-india/ ; official Act text: https://www.indiacode.nic.in/
rules.retrieved_snippet: Section 42 mandates that people with disabilities must have equal ICT access, including websites, digital content, and electronic media. Section 46 requires that all government documents, services, and public information that are digitally available must be accessible. The GIGW enforces WCAG 2.1 Level AA compliance for public-sector platforms. Organizations that fail to comply may face penalties ranging from INR 10,000 to 500,000.

rules.source: Information Technology Act, 2000 (Central Act 21 of 2000), ss. 43 and 66 — https://www.indiacode.nic.in/handle/123456789/13116 (act PDF: https://www.indiacode.nic.in/bitstream/123456789/1999/1/A2000-21%20(1).pdf)
rules.retrieved_snippet: Search summary only (indiacode pages returned HTTP 403 on fetch): Act received assent 9 June 2000; s.43 is titled "Penalty and compensation for damage to computer, computer system, etc."; s.66 "Computer Related Offences" (2008 consolidated text) applies to a person who dishonestly or fraudulently does any act in s.43, punishable with imprisonment up to three years or fine or both; s.66A is listed as omitted.

rules.source: Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 (notified 25 February 2021 under s.87 of the IT Act, 2000) — gazette copy https://www.thc.nic.in/Central Governmental Rules/IT(Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021.pdf
rules.retrieved_snippet: Search summary only (PDF not text-extractable on fetch): MeitY notified the Rules on 25 February 2021 under s.87(1) and s.87(2)(z),(zg) of the IT Act 2000; they cover intermediaries, digital news publishers and OTT platforms, replaced the 2011 intermediary rules, and Part III (Code of Ethics) is administered by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

rules.source: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (Act No. 45 of 2023), s.111 — https://www.mha.gov.in/sites/default/files/2024-04/250883_english_01042024.pdf
rules.retrieved_snippet: Search summary only (official PDF returned HTTP 403; s.111 description came from secondary legal sites): BNS is Act 45 of 2023, assent 25 December 2023, in force 1 July 2024 per a High Court order (BNS repeals the IPC via s.358); s.111 is a new organised-crime offence defined as continuing unlawful activity by a group/syndicate using violence, intimidation or other unlawful means for material gain.
